title: Temozolomide for recurrent or progressive glioma
context_label: Adults with grade III or IV malignant glioma recurring or progressing after standard therapy under NCCP 00342.
purpose: Temozolomide is used to help control a high-grade glioma that has returned or progressed after previous treatment. The team considers previous medicines, current symptoms, scans and your priorities when deciding whether it is suitable.
schedule_summary: Take temozolomide once daily on Days 1–5, then no temozolomide on Days 6–28. Repeat only when your team authorises the next 28-day cycle. The course is reviewed for benefit and toxicity rather than a fixed six-cycle finish.
scope_note: Adults with grade III or IV malignant glioma recurring or progressing after standard therapy under NCCP 00342. Use the plan matched to your diagnosis and phase; do not borrow another glioma schedule.

indication_text: Adults with grade III or IV malignant glioma recurring or progressing after standard therapy under NCCP 00342.
phases_title: Treatment days → recovery and tests → review
phases_note: The team confirms each phase and prescription. Do not use the capsule dose or test schedule from a different phase.
timeline_note: The cycle view shows relative treatment days, not a prediction of when symptoms will peak. Serious symptoms can occur at any time, including rest days.
safety_note: Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice, including on treatment rest days. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow the emergency instructions in any established seizure rescue plan.
teachback: Can you show the days for each medicine, the current phase, your next blood tests and whom to call for fever, vomiting or new neurological symptoms?
consent_support: Discuss treatment intent, evidence and alternatives; phase-specific schedules; blood and organ monitoring; infection, nausea, fertility and pregnancy precautions; practical support and any unlicensed use. Keep the separate radiotherapy consent and medication plans where applicable.
urgent_extra: Use your written emergency plan even on days without chemotherapy. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow any existing seizure rescue plan. Promptly report worsening headache, repeated vomiting, cough, breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin or eyes, or inability to drink. A held chemotherapy dose must not be restarted without instructions.

agents.name: Temozolomide
agents.explanation: Temozolomide crosses into the brain and creates chemical changes in DNA. If the damage cannot be repaired, a cell may stop dividing or die. Healthy blood-forming cells can also be affected, which helps explain blood-count changes, infection and bleeding risks. Nausea prevention and liver monitoring are important too.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, persistent vomiting, new breathing symptoms or yellow skin/eyes. Keep blood and liver tests even after capsule days finish.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Rash and rare severe skin reactions
Fertility effects and harm to a pregnancy

passport_visit_note: Record the current phase, every prescribed medicine and treatment day, doses held, safety tests, symptoms, MRI review and the next authorised treatment. A stamp records treatment; it does not authorise the next dose.
anatomy_note: Selected regimen-specific effects use the retained detailed body illustration. Brain symptoms may come from the tumour or treatment; blood, skin and nerve effects are not confined to one point. This is not a prediction or the complete side-effect list.
anatomy: Fatigue or headache may occur. New seizures, sudden weakness, speech difficulty or loss of consciousness need emergency help.
Report mouth soreness, ulcers or reduced intake. Keep gentle mouth care and ask for help before eating or drinking becomes difficult.
Counts can fall after capsule days finish. Fever, sudden illness, bruising or bleeding needs urgent advice; keep all blood tests.
New cough, fever or breathlessness needs prompt review. The team assesses PJP risk, especially with steroids or low lymphocyte counts.
Liver injury may appear during or after treatment. Attend liver tests and report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or unusual itching.
Take anti-sickness medicine as prescribed. Call for repeated vomiting, inability to drink, severe constipation or abdominal pain.
Rash or hair changes may occur. Blistering, peeling skin or a rash with fever needs urgent medical advice.
Discuss contraception and fertility before starting. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Ask for the written medicine-specific precautions.

phases.label: Repeated 28-day cycles with individual review
phases.detail: Take temozolomide once daily on Days 1–5, then no temozolomide on Days 6–28. Repeat only when your team authorises the next 28-day cycle. The course is reviewed for benefit and toxicity rather than a fixed six-cycle finish.

timeline.label: Temozolomide once daily
timeline.text: Use the current phase prescription, fasting and with the prescribed nausea plan.

timeline.label: No temozolomide capsules
timeline.text: Recovery, symptoms and blood/liver tests; restart only when authorised.

timeline.label: Day 22 blood count
timeline.text: EMA recommends a count around Day 22 and follow-up until recovery.

timeline.label: Safety throughout the cycle
timeline.text: Fever, bleeding, neurological or breathing symptoms need prompt advice.

day_groups.title: Five daily capsule doses
day_groups.body: Check the prescribed capsule strengths and number each day. Take fasting with the anti-sickness plan.
day_groups.action: Do not use leftover capsules to change the dose or replace a vomited dose.

day_groups.title: No temozolomide; recovery continues
day_groups.body: Rest days allow recovery but blood counts can still fall. Continue other medicines only as individually prescribed.
day_groups.action: Contact the team for fever, sudden illness, bruising or persistent vomiting.

day_groups.title: Blood count and next-cycle decision
day_groups.body: Have the Day 22 blood count and any follow-up blood tests arranged. Before the next cycle, the team reviews counts, kidney/liver tests and symptoms.
day_groups.action: Do not start the next cycle just because the calendar reaches Day 1.

chronology_notes.title: Dose changes belong to the current phase
chronology_notes.text: Daily chemoradiotherapy and five-day cycles use different doses. Check the label and phase with the pharmacist whenever a new supply is issued.

chronology_notes.title: No replacement after vomiting
chronology_notes.text: If you vomit after a temozolomide dose, do not take a second dose that day. For a missed dose, follow the pharmacist’s written instructions or contact the team; never double up.

chronology_notes.title: Effects can be delayed
chronology_notes.text: Blood counts and liver effects can change after capsule days finish or after the last cycle. Keep the follow-up tests and emergency plan.

administration_text: Take the exact temozolomide capsule strengths and number on your pharmacy label, once daily when prescribed, on an empty stomach. Swallow whole with water; do not open, chew or crush. Ask the pharmacist to write the fasting interval and anti-sickness timing. Different phase doses are not interchangeable.

support.title: Nausea prevention
support.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids.

support.title: PJP infection prevention
support.text: The team reviews infection and PJP risk, especially with steroids, low lymphocytes or prolonged treatment. A separate prevention prescription may be needed; do not assume the mandatory concurrent-radiotherapy plan automatically applies to this five-day schedule.

support.title: Bowels, food and fluids
support.text: Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting.

support.title: Steroid and seizure plans
support.text: If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.

monitoring_summary: Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and hepatitis B screening. NCCP requires blood count, kidney and liver tests on Day 1 of every cycle. EMA additionally advises a Day 22 blood count, then weekly until recovery, and liver tests after every cycle. Liver injury can develop after treatment stops. MRI and neurological review follow your individual plan.

sections.title: Taking the treatment
sections.text: Take the exact temozolomide capsule strengths and number on your pharmacy label, once daily when prescribed, on an empty stomach. Swallow whole with water; do not open, chew or crush. Ask the pharmacist to write the fasting interval and anti-sickness timing. Different phase doses are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Missed or vomited medicine
sections.text: If you vomit after temozolomide, do not take another dose that day. For a missed dose, use your pharmacist’s written instructions or call before taking it late; do not double a dose. Never replace a dose held for toxicity.

sections.title: Medicine and supplement review
sections.text: Bring an up-to-date list of all medicines, including steroids, seizure medicines, anticoagulants, non-prescription treatments, vitamins and herbs. Ask before starting something new. Keep a record of all dose changes.

sections.title: Storage and handling
sections.text: Keep capsules in their original labelled packs, away from children. Do not open, crush or chew. If swallowing or medicine organisation is difficult, contact the team before the next dose and agree safe help. Return unused chemotherapy to the pharmacy.

sections.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
sections.text: Treatment can harm a pregnancy and may affect fertility. Discuss fertility preservation, contraception for patients and partners, and the required period after the final dose before starting. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Ask the team for written, medicine-specific advice.

MRI and neurological review follow your individual plan.

evidence.title: Evidence must match the recurrent setting
evidence.intro: This is the NCCP recurrent or progressive high-grade glioma regimen, not the newly diagnosed chemoradiation schedule.
evidence.population: Adults with recurrent or progressive grade III or IV malignant glioma after standard treatment.
evidence.interpretation: The treatment aim and likely benefit depend on the integrated diagnosis, prior chemotherapy, previous response and current condition.
limitations: Survival figures from newly diagnosed glioblastoma chemoradiation must not be used as estimates for recurrent disease.
The source schedule is reviewed until progression or unacceptable toxicity; the six-cycle row in its dose table does not establish a universal maximum course.

chapters.title: Your treatment and its purpose
chapters.intro: Use the regimen and phase agreed with your team.

chapters.title: Tests, urgent symptoms and follow-up
chapters.intro: Keep planned tests and know how to get help.

items.title: When to seek help
items.text: Use your written emergency plan even on days without chemotherapy. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow any existing seizure rescue plan. Promptly report worsening headache, repeated vomiting, cough, breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin or eyes, or inability to drink. A held chemotherapy dose must not be restarted without instructions.

items.title: Support medicines
items.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids. The team reviews infection and PJP risk, especially with steroids, low lymphocytes or prolonged treatment. A separate prevention prescription may be needed; do not assume the mandatory concurrent-radiotherapy plan automatically applies to this five-day schedule. Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting. If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.

items.title: A delay is a treatment decision
items.text: Blood counts, organ tests or symptoms may mean a dose is held, reduced or stopped. This is a safety decision, not a reason to take extra capsules later. Ask which medicines change, which support medicines continue and when the next assessment is due.

items.title: After the final dose
items.text: Agree follow-up blood tests, symptom review, MRI timing and who to contact. Continue to report new problems; effects can outlast chemotherapy. Keep your medicine list and written plan current.

chapters.title: Understanding your particular glioma
chapters.intro: Your diagnosis includes the tumour’s cells, molecular findings and behaviour, not just the word brain cancer.

items.title: The name and location
items.text: A glioma is a tumour arising in the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different types. Cancer that travels to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and follows a different pathway.

items.title: Grade is not the same as stage
items.text: Glioma reports combine the tumour type, grade and molecular findings. Grade is not a measure of spread around the body: a grade 4 brain tumour does not mean body-wide metastases. Ask your specialist to explain older terms in your records.

items.title: IDH and 1p/19q
items.text: Changes in the IDH genes and loss of chromosome regions 1p and 19q help classify certain gliomas. The pattern of results matters. These are usually tumour-sample tests; they do not by themselves show that a change runs in the family.

items.title: MGMT promoter methylation
items.text: The MGMT gene makes a protein that repairs a particular type of DNA damage. Methylation in its control region can reduce that repair and inform discussion of temozolomide benefit. This is a tumour-tissue result, not a blood marker or a personal survival percentage.

items.title: A useful diagnosis record
items.text: Keep the exact pathology diagnosis, sample date, grade and available molecular results together. Label a result as pending or not tested when appropriate. Ask whether further pathology review would affect the plan.

chapters.title: Tests and scans: what each one tells you
chapters.intro: Safety blood tests, tumour tissue tests and MRI answer different questions.

items.title: Safety blood tests
items.text: A full blood count measures red cells, white cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests assess other aspects of treatment safety. Follow the blood-test schedule even when you feel well or the scan is reassuring.

items.title: MRI and neurological review
items.text: MRI gives detailed pictures of the brain. The team also checks symptoms, movement, speech, thinking and daily function. Before scanning, tell staff about implants, metal, kidney problems or previous contrast reactions, and ask for help if the scan worries you.

items.title: Changes on a scan need interpretation
items.text: Treatment-related changes can resemble tumour growth on MRI; this is called pseudoprogression. The specialist interprets the scan with symptoms and may need another scan or further assessment. Report worsening symptoms promptly rather than assuming a scan change is harmless.

items.title: An individual follow-up timetable
items.text: Record the next MRI and the contact who will explain it. Your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous results determine the interval. Other scans or blood markers are ordered for a specific reason, not automatically before every cycle.

items.title: Keep results with decisions
items.text: Mark tests as booked, done and reviewed so the next action is clear. Contact the named service about a missing result. Do not change chemotherapy or steroids in response to a report without instructions.

chapters.title: Brain symptoms, medicines and when to call
chapters.intro: Symptoms may reflect the tumour, swelling, treatment, another medicine or a separate illness.

items.title: Know your usual symptoms
items.text: Before treatment, note your usual walking, strength, speech, sight, memory, sleep and seizure pattern. Record new changes and their timing. A trusted person can help if you want them involved.

items.title: Urgent neurological changes
items.text: Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice, including on treatment rest days. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow the emergency instructions in any established seizure rescue plan.

items.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
items.text: Steroids may reduce swelling around a brain tumour. If needed, ask for a written dose, review date and reduction plan; do not stop suddenly or adjust the dose yourself. Report infection symptoms, marked thirst, weakness or troublesome sleep or mood changes.

items.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
items.text: Take prescribed seizure medicine on its own schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and how to manage a breakthrough seizure. Do not switch or stop it yourself. Anyone giving a rescue medicine needs the personal instructions and training.

items.title: Safety at home and outside
items.text: Discuss driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery with your team, taking account of symptoms and seizures. Individual medical and licensing advice is needed. Occupational therapy can help make daily routines safer.

chapters.title: Your overall treatment plan and choices
chapters.intro: Treatment should account for the tumour and the life you want to lead.

items.title: Understand the sequence
items.text: Place biopsy or surgery, radiotherapy, medicines and follow-up on one plan. Concurrent means treatments overlap; adjuvant means treatment follows the main treatment. A new phase can require different doses, tests and support medicines.

items.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
items.text: Ask what treatment can reasonably achieve for your tumour and which effects matter most to you. Discuss benefits, burdens, alternatives and the reasons for a pause or stop.

items.title: Put evidence in context
items.text: A study result applies to a particular group, diagnosis and schedule. Older studies may use different tumour names. Ask which evidence fits your plan; an average cannot forecast your response or lifespan.

items.title: Discuss options available to you
items.text: Ask about suitable trials, another specialist opinion and other treatment or symptom-care options. Your multidisciplinary team explains what is appropriate and available for you.

items.title: Make room for your priorities
items.text: Bring up thinking, independence, family time, work and the side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for time, written notes or a supporter if that helps you weigh the choices.

chapters.title: Living well, rehabilitation and support
chapters.intro: Practical and symptom support can begin alongside anticancer treatment.

items.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
items.text: Tell the team about changes in memory, language, attention, sight or planning. Rehabilitation can involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or psychology. Ask for practical help with routines and medicines.

items.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
items.text: Use your prescribed nausea and bowel plan and report problems early. Ask for dietitian help if intake or weight falls. Adapt movement to your balance and strength, and ask the team to assess fatigue that disrupts daily life.

items.title: Emotional support and carers
items.text: Tell the team about changes in mood, behaviour or coping. Patients and carers may each need psychological or practical support. Agree who can receive information and ask for help before caring becomes overwhelming.

items.title: Work, transport and finances
items.text: Plan travel, time away from work, caring duties and help with appointments. A nurse or social worker can identify practical support; agree who can help with tablets if needed.

items.title: Supportive care and future wishes
items.text: Supportive and palliative care can help manage symptoms while treatment continues. When you are ready, discuss future care preferences and whom you want involved. Ask your team to help document these wishes.

items.title: Information that works on paper
items.text: Keep the latest paper schedule, medicine list, results plan and emergency contacts together. The treatment card helps others identify your regimen. It supports, but does not replace, the prescription and emergency instructions.

questions.q: What is my exact diagnosis, grade and relevant molecular result?
questions.a: Ask for the integrated pathology wording and an explanation of IDH, 1p/19q and MGMT where relevant. The diagnosis and treatment history guide how this regimen applies to you.

questions.q: Which phase and capsule calendar am I on now?
questions.a: Take temozolomide once daily on Days 1–5, then no temozolomide on Days 6–28. Repeat only when your team authorises the next 28-day cycle. The course is reviewed for benefit and toxicity rather than a fixed six-cycle finish.

questions.q: Which tests must happen before I can take the next dose?
questions.a: Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and hepatitis B screening. NCCP requires blood count, kidney and liver tests on Day 1 of every cycle. EMA additionally advises a Day 22 blood count, then weekly until recovery, and liver tests after every cycle. Liver injury can develop after treatment stops. MRI and neurological review follow your individual plan.

questions.q: Who helps with seizures, steroids, memory or daily tasks?
questions.a: Ask for a named contact, written seizure and steroid plans if prescribed, and rehabilitation or practical support. Agree who can help you organise treatment.

questions.q: Which symptoms mean contact the team today?
questions.a: Use your written emergency plan even on days without chemotherapy. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow any existing seizure rescue plan. Promptly report worsening headache, repeated vomiting, cough, breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin or eyes, or inability to drink. A held chemotherapy dose must not be restarted without instructions.

questions.q: When will we review the benefit and my priorities?
questions.a: Ask for the next clinical and MRI review, how treatment effects will be distinguished from growth, and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping treatment.
